summary: Defines SNMP MIB objects for monitoring and controlling iFCP gateways and their sessions. iFCP (RFC 4172) provides Fibre Channel fabric functionality on an IP network. It is standards-track and was replaced by RFC 6173.

plainLanguage.summary: A control panel for checking on gadgets that carry storage-network traffic over the ordinary internet.

subtitle: SNMP objects for managing Fibre Channel storage traffic over IP

tldr.problem: Storage networks using Fibre Channel need a way to move data over regular IP networks, but operators need standardized management tools to monitor and configure these gateways.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines an SNMP MIB module for iFCP gateways that supplies objects for configuring local gateway instances, managing iFCP sessions between gateways, and collecting statistics on session performance.
tldr.outcome: Network operators can now monitor and manage iFCP gateway instances and sessions using SNMP, collecting statistics on storage traffic and configuring parameters like timeout values. RFC 6173 later updated this specification.

today: RFC 4369 is a Proposed Standard. It was obsoleted by RFC 6173, which updates the iFCP MIB specification.

sections.title: Introduction and Overview
sections.content:
RFC 4369 defines an SNMP MIB module for monitoring and managing iFCP (Internet Fibre Channel Protocol) gateways. iFCP is a protocol that lets Fibre Channel storage networks communicate over regular IP networks by encapsulating Fibre Channel frames in TCP/IP packets.

An iFCP gateway sits at the boundary between a Fibre Channel storage domain and an IP network. It translates between the two technologies: on one side it connects to Fibre Channel devices like disk arrays and tape libraries; on the other side it sends data to peer gateways over the IP network. The MIB module allows SNMP management systems to monitor multiple local gateway instances and their sessions to remote gateways.
sections.plainLanguage: iFCP gateways are translators between storage systems and the internet. This MIB lets you watch and tune those translators.

sections.title: MIB Organization
sections.content:
The iFCP MIB module is organized into three main sections: local gateway instance management, session management, and session statistics.

The local gateway instance section provides configuration and status information for each iFCP gateway running on the managed device. A single device can host multiple independent gateways, each with both Fibre Channel and IP interfaces. Default parameters like the IP Time-Out Value (IP_TOV), which specifies how long an encapsulated frame can travel through the IP network before expiring, are set per gateway.

The session management section describes active iFCP sessions between this gateway and peer gateways. Each session carries storage traffic between a Fibre Channel device (N_PORT) on one side and an N_PORT on a peer gateway on the other. Sessions inherit the gateway's default IP_TOV but can override it with session-specific values, as well as configure the Liveness Test Interval (LTI), which ensures the TCP connection stays alive.

The statistics section augments the session management table with counters on frame exchanges, errors, and other performance metrics.
sections.plainLanguage: The MIB divides management into three parts: configuring the gateways themselves, managing the connections (sessions) between gateways, and counting what happens on each connection.

sections.title: Gateway and Session Configuration
sections.content:
Each local iFCP gateway instance is identified by a unique index and can be configured with:

Gateway-level settings: A textual description, an optional link to the physical entity (via the ENTITY-MIB), default IP_TOV, default Liveness Test Interval, address translation mode (static or dynamic), and whether broadcast forwarding is supported on Fibre Channel.

Session parameters: For each iFCP session, the MIB provides the local and remote Fibre Channel port identifiers, the IP address and TCP port of the remote gateway, the current session state (down, openPending, or open), session-specific IP_TOV override, and session-specific Liveness Test Interval.

The MIB also provides optional integration with other standard MIBs: the Fibre Channel Management MIB (RFC 4044) for Fibre Channel-specific objects, the Interfaces Group MIB (RFC 2863) for interface statistics, and the Entity MIB for physical entity mapping.
sections.plainLanguage: You set a default timeout for each gateway, but you can change it per session. You tell it which storage systems are on the Fibre Channel side, which gateways are on the IP side, and whether the connection is up.

sections.title: Statistics and Monitoring
sections.content:
The iFCP MIB provides performance counters in two formats: standard 32-bit counters and 64-bit high-capacity counters for systems that send a high volume of frames.

Statistics are collected per session and include the number of FC frames sent and received, the number of bytes transferred in each direction, the number of TCP connection establishments, TCP connection resets and timeouts, and various error conditions such as frames dropped, invalid frames, and encapsulation errors. These counters help operators detect congestion, session instability, or configuration problems.

Because iFCP carries storage traffic, which may be business-critical, these statistics are essential for troubleshooting and capacity planning.
sections.plainLanguage: The MIB counts how many messages go through each connection, how many errors happen, and whether the connection is stable.
